facts.claim: NGINX sends requests to its servers in round-robin fashion unless another method is set: round robin is its default.
NGINX’s least-connected method sends the next request to the server with the fewest active connections, which spreads load more fairly when some requests take longer.
With server weights of 3, 1 and 1, NGINX sends 3 of every 5 new requests to the first server and one to each of the others.
Mitzenmacher showed that letting each arrival pick the less loaded of 2 random servers gives exponential improvements in time spent over picking 1 at random (IEEE TPDS, 2001).
Envoy’s least request balancer picks 2 random available hosts by default and prefers the one with fewer active requests, a method it calls P2C (power of two choices).
An AWS Application Load Balancer checks each target every 30 seconds by default and takes it out of service after 2 failed checks in a row, its default unhealthy threshold.
If every target fails its health checks at once, an AWS Application Load Balancer fails open and sends requests to all of them.

Microsoft researchers named subtle faults that are not outright crashes gray failure, and traced them to differential observability: a system’s failure detectors may not notice what its users feel (HotOS, 2017).
NGINX’s ip-hash method keeps a client’s requests on the same server, a sticky or persistent session, except when that server is unavailable.
Google’s Dean and Barroso argue that rare slow moments, harmless in a small system, come to dominate the latency of a large one (Communications of the ACM, 2013).
Dean and Barroso describe hedged requests: send the same request to a second server once the first has waited longer than most requests do, and use whichever answers first.
